## What changed

Everything here came from one real instance: GitLab **13.12.15** on Ubuntu
20.04 behind a SOCKS5 proxy — the long climb this tool exists for, run for the
first time by someone other than its author.

**`apt-cache madison` answers from local lists, and the diagnostic blamed the
proxy for it.** Every rung passed — TCP, SOCKS handshake, CONNECT, TLS with a
real certificate, HTTP 200 — and then the last rung said "apt sees no version:
no reason given". There was no reason to give: `apt-cache` reads
`/var/lib/apt/lists` and never touches the network, so with no successful
`apt-get update` for the repository it exits 0 with empty stdout *and* empty
stderr. Verified against a live apt. While that read as a proxy failure, the
one thing actually missing was an `apt-get update`. There is now a separate
rung for "the repository is configured but its lists were never fetched", and
the old rung no longer confesses to having nothing to say. `check` and `plan`
say it too, instead of pointing only at `proxy test`.

Also verified on a live apt, because the whole configuration rests on it:
**apt does support `socks5h://` for an https repository**. A local SOCKS5
server logged `CONNECT packages.gitlab.com:443` and apt fetched `InRelease`
through the tunnel, which means the proxy settings this tool writes are the
working kind, not the plausible kind.

**`scope :queued` only exists from 14.0, so the migration check failed on
every version this tool is meant to climb out of.** In 13.11–13.12 the model
carries a single scope, `queue_order`, with statuses declared as a Rails enum —
which does give `.active`, `.paused` and `.failed`. Two API eras, and the route
from 13.x passes through both, so the query now adapts through `respond_to?`
rather than guessing from a version number: on a nineteen-step climb the
instance version changes under you nineteen times. Any *other* `NoMethodError`
still propagates instead of becoming a silent "no migrations pending". The
query is now executed by real Ruby against stubs of all three model eras,
because a string interpreted by someone else's interpreter cannot be checked
any other way.

**The PostgreSQL barrier was read off the final target, which blocked a climb
that could have started immediately.** On 13.12 with PostgreSQL 12.6 the check
demanded 16.5 — what 18.11 needs — and refused to proceed. Twice wrong: the
first ten steps run on PostgreSQL 12 quite happily, and `gitlab-ctl pg-upgrade`
on 13.12 cannot produce 16.5 under any circumstances, because the required
versions arrive with the packages along the way. The barrier is now located per
step: on the first step it stops, further along it warns and names the step to
beat. The two real gates are 17.0.0 (PostgreSQL 14) and 18.0.0 (PostgreSQL 16),
both documented with "package upgrades are aborted".

A related correction, made and then reverted in the same day: minimum
PostgreSQL versions for 14.x and 15.x were briefly added from the package
version table. Those columns are what the package *ships* and upgrades *to*,
not a prerequisite — the note on the 14.0 row is about repmgr. Requiring 12.7
of an instance running 13.12 would have stopped this climb on step one, since
12.7 is what 14.0 itself brings.

**`compareVersions` returned 0 — "equal" — for an object it could not read.**
`undefined - 16` is `NaN`, `NaN` is falsy in an `||` chain, and the expression
fell through to `0 - 0`. An unparsed version therefore matched every range, and
the last row of the requirements table won: a perfectly healthy instance was
told it needed PostgreSQL 17. It now throws.

And two tests were passing without testing anything: a missing `execFileSync`
import raised `ReferenceError`, my own `catch { return; }` swallowed it, and
both "ruby" tests reported success in 0.14 ms having never started an
interpreter. The skip now catches exactly `ENOENT` and nothing else.

**Finding your Telegram chat id no longer means doing it by hand.** It used to
take `curl`, `grep` over JSON, and your bot token typed onto a command line
where `ps` can read it — and the point of notifications is that a nineteen-step
climb does not need you at the terminal. With the token already in the config,
`gitlab-upgrade notify chat` waits for you to press Start in the bot chat and
answers *in that chat* with its id, which is where you are looking anyway. It
also prints it, and with `--yes` writes it to the config. It never picks for
you when several people have written to the bot: silently choosing one is how
upgrade reports end up going to a stranger. A webhook on the bot (which makes
`getUpdates` impossible) is reported as its own diagnosis rather than as
"nobody wrote".

And a delivery failure is no longer mistaken for a delivered message. Telegram
answers a bad token with a perfectly successful HTTP request carrying 401, so
nothing threw and nothing was reported: every notification across nineteen
steps would have vanished in silence. Non-2xx replies are now named, with the
bot token and webhook URL redacted out of the message — the token sits in the
request URL, and these lines go to the system journal.

Both paths were verified against the live `api.telegram.org` through a real
SOCKS5 proxy, not only against stubs.

Lastly, the project's own linter could not see a syntax error: `a ?? b || c`
without parentheses passed it and failed at runtime. It parses every file now.
